claim: SARM1 is a protein with critical NADase activity.
source: SARM1, a protein with critical NADase activity, is a central executioner in a conserved programme of axon degeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript to prior work establishing SARM1's NADase activity.

claim: SARM1 is a central executioner in a conserved programme of axon degeneration.
source: SARM1, a protein with critical NADase activity, is a central executioner in a conserved programme of axon degeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior research throughout the manuscript.

claim: Seven rare missense or in-frame microdeletion human SARM1 variant alleles were found in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) or other motor nerve disorders.
source: We report seven rare missense or in-frame microdeletion human SARM1 variant alleles in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) or other motor nerve disorders that alter the SARM1 auto-inhibitory ARM domain and constitutively hyperactivate SARM1 NADase activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript including Tables 1 and 2 and Figures 2-4.

claim: The seven SARM1 variants alter the SARM1 auto-inhibitory ARM domain.
source: We report seven rare missense or in-frame microdeletion human SARM1 variant alleles in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) or other motor nerve disorders that alter the SARM1 auto-inhibitory ARM domain and constitutively hyperactivate SARM1 NADase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the location of the variants shown in Figure 1 and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The seven SARM1 variants constitutively hyperactivate SARM1 NADase activity.
source: We report seven rare missense or in-frame microdeletion human SARM1 variant alleles in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) or other motor nerve disorders that alter the SARM1 auto-inhibitory ARM domain and constitutively hyperactivate SARM1 NADase activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated by NADase activity assays shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The constitutive NADase activity of the seven variants is similar to that of SARM1 lacking the entire ARM domain.
source: The constitutive NADase activity of these seven variants is similar to that of SARM1 lacking the entire ARM domain and greatly exceeds the activity of wild-type SARM1, even in the presence of nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), its physiological activator.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by NADase activity assays comparing variants to SAM-TIR fragment in Figure 3B.

claim: The constitutive NADase activity of the seven variants greatly exceeds the activity of wild-type SARM1, even in the presence of nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN).
source: The constitutive NADase activity of these seven variants is similar to that of SARM1 lacking the entire ARM domain and greatly exceeds the activity of wild-type SARM1, even in the presence of nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), its physiological activator.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by NADase activity assays in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: The rise in constitutive activity alone is enough to promote neuronal degeneration in response to otherwise non-harmful, mild stress.
source: This rise in constitutive activity alone is enough to promote neuronal degeneration in response to otherwise non-harmful, mild stress.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by experiments in primary neurons shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The strong gain-of-function alleles are completely patient-specific in the cohorts studied.
source: Importantly, these strong gain-of-function alleles are completely patient-specific in the cohorts studied and show a highly significant association with disease at the single gene level.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the distribution data shown in Figure 8 and Table 3.

claim: The strong gain-of-function alleles show a highly significant association with disease at the single gene level.
source: Importantly, these strong gain-of-function alleles are completely patient-specific in the cohorts studied and show a highly significant association with disease at the single gene level.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by statistical analyses described in the Results section showing burden test and SKAT-O p = 0.00017.

claim: A neighbouring, more common SARM1 intragenic single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) has previously shown genome-wide significant association with ALS.
source: These findings of disease-associated coding variants that alter SARM1 function build on previously reported genome-wide significant association with ALS for a neighbouring, more common SARM1 intragenic single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) to support a contributory role of SARM1 in these disorders.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior GWAS studies (Fogh et al., 2014; van Rheenen et al., 2016).

claim: There is broad phenotypic heterogeneity among patients with these alleles.
source: A broad phenotypic heterogeneity and variable age-of-onset of disease among patients with these alleles also raises intriguing questions about the pathogenic mechanism of hyperactive SARM1 variants.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by clinical information presented in Table 4.

claim: There is variable age-of-onset of disease among patients with these alleles.
source: A broad phenotypic heterogeneity and variable age-of-onset of disease among patients with these alleles also raises intriguing questions about the pathogenic mechanism of hyperactive SARM1 variants.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by clinical information presented in Table 4.

claim: SARM1 is required for axon degeneration after injury, in response to toxins and other insults, and in several models of neurodegenerative disease.
source: The toll-like receptor adaptor protein SARM1 is required for axon degeneration after injury, in response to toxins and other insults, and in several models of neurodegenerative disease (Conforti et al., 2014; Coleman and Höke, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The interplay between pro-degenerative SARM1 and its upstream, pro-survival regulator NMNAT2 is critical in many situations.
source: In many of these situations, the intimate interplay between pro-degenerative SARM1 (sterile alpha and TIR motif containing protein 1) (Osterloh et al., 2012; Gerdts et al., 2013) and its upstream, pro-survival regulator NMNAT2 (nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferase 2) (Gilley and Coleman, 2010; Gilley et al., 2015) is critical and most likely involves a disruption to normal nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) homeostasis (Gerdts et al., 2016; Figley and DiAntonio, 2020) or related metabolites (Angeletti et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NMNAT2 is one of three NMNAT isoforms that catalyse the last step in NAD+ biosynthesis.
source: NMNAT2 is one of three NMNAT isoforms that catalyse the last step in NAD+ biosynthesis and is the predominant NMNAT in axons.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: NMNAT2 is the predominant NMNAT in axons.
source: NMNAT2 is one of three NMNAT isoforms that catalyse the last step in NAD+ biosynthesis and is the predominant NMNAT in axons.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The SARM1 TIR domain has a critical NAD+ consuming multifunctional glycohydrolase (NADase) activity.
source: The SARM1 TIR domain has a critical NAD+ consuming multifunctional glycohydrolase (NADase) activity (Essuman et al., 2017; Horsefield et al., 2019; Wan et al., 2019) and, intriguingly, NMNAT substrate, NMN, and its product, NAD+, can both influence this activity: NMN activates SARM1 NADase by binding to an allosteric site in the auto-inhibitory ARM domain of the enzyme (Zhao et al., 2019; Figley et al., 2021), whereas NAD+ can oppose this activation by competing for binding to the same site (Jiang et al., 2020; Sporny et al., 2020; Figley et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NMN activates SARM1 NADase by binding to an allosteric site in the auto-inhibitory ARM domain of the enzyme.
source: The SARM1 TIR domain has a critical NAD+ consuming multifunctional glycohydrolase (NADase) activity (Essuman et al., 2017; Horsefield et al., 2019; Wan et al., 2019) and, intriguingly, NMNAT substrate, NMN, and its product, NAD+, can both influence this activity: NMN activates SARM1 NADase by binding to an allosteric site in the auto-inhibitory ARM domain of the enzyme (Zhao et al., 2019; Figley et al., 2021), whereas NAD+ can oppose this activation by competing for binding to the same site (Jiang et al., 2020; Sporny et al., 2020; Figley et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NAD+ can oppose SARM1 NADase activation by competing for binding to the same allosteric site as NMN.
source: The SARM1 TIR domain has a critical NAD+ consuming multifunctional glycohydrolase (NADase) activity (Essuman et al., 2017; Horsefield et al., 2019; Wan et al., 2019) and, intriguingly, NMNAT substrate, NMN, and its product, NAD+, can both influence this activity: NMN activates SARM1 NADase by binding to an allosteric site in the auto-inhibitory ARM domain of the enzyme (Zhao et al., 2019; Figley et al., 2021), whereas NAD+ can oppose this activation by competing for binding to the same site (Jiang et al., 2020; Sporny et al., 2020; Figley et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rising NMN and declining NAD+ as a consequence of loss of NMNAT2 in damaged axons leads directly to activation of SARM1 NADase.
source: Rising NMN and declining NAD+ as a consequence of loss of very short-lived NMNAT2 in damaged axons (Di Stefano et al., 2015) thus leads directly to activation of SARM1 NADase and a self-reinforcing NAD+ decline that represents one possible cause of degeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: SARM1 can promote neuronal cell death under certain conditions.
source: As well as its established role in axons, SARM1 can promote neuronal cell death under certain conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Recent studies suggest direct involvement of SARM1 in neuronal cell death in some situations, including photoreceptor loss in models of retinal degeneration and Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA).
source: However, recent studies do suggest direct involvement of SARM1 in neuronal cell death in some situations, including photoreceptor loss in models of retinal degeneration and Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA) (Ozaki et al., 2020; Sasaki et al., 2020) and as a result of Vacor neurotoxicity when specifically applied to cell bodies (Loreto et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to recent research.

claim: Biallelic NMNAT2 loss-of-function (LoF) variants have been associated with two rare polyneuropathies.
source: To date, biallelic NMNAT2 loss-of-function (LoF) variants have been associated with two rare polyneuropathies that broadly resemble the corresponding mouse models (Gilley et al., 2013; Gilley et al., 2019; Huppke et al., 2019; Lukacs et al., 2019), and NMNAT1 mutations cause photoreceptor loss in LCA via a mechanism involving SARM1 (Sasaki et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NMNAT1 mutations cause photoreceptor loss in LCA via a mechanism involving SARM1.
source: To date, biallelic NMNAT2 loss-of-function (LoF) variants have been associated with two rare polyneuropathies that broadly resemble the corresponding mouse models (Gilley et al., 2013; Gilley et al., 2019; Huppke et al., 2019; Lukacs et al., 2019), and NMNAT1 mutations cause photoreceptor loss in LCA via a mechanism involving SARM1 (Sasaki et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Genome wide association studies (GWAS) have linked the SARM1 chromosomal locus, including an intragenic SNP, to sporadic ALS.
source: While no firm association between SARM1 variation and human disease has yet been established, genome wide association studies (GWAS) have linked the SARM1 chromosomal locus, including an intragenic SNP, to sporadic ALS (Fogh et al., 2014; van Rheenen et al., 2016), although whether SARM1 is the causative gene is not known.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior GWAS studies.

claim: SARM1-dependent death mechanisms have been found to play a significant role in a mutant TDP-43 model of ALS.
source: Recently, SARM1-dependent death mechanisms have been found to play a significant role in a mutant TDP-43 model of ALS (White et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: TDP-43 aggregation is an almost universal pathologic feature in ALS.
source: This is important as TDP-43 aggregation is an almost universal pathologic feature in ALS (Arai et al., 2006; Neumann et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Removal of SARM1 does not alleviate motor neuron degeneration in a SOD1 model of ALS.
source: While removal of SARM1 does not alleviate motor neuron degeneration in a SOD1 model of ALS (Peters et al., 2018), this could be explained by the finding that TDP-43 aggregation is usually not seen in ALS linked to SOD1 or FUS mutations (Mackenzie et al., 2007; Maekawa et al., 2009; McAlary et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: TDP-43 aggregation is usually not seen in ALS linked to SOD1 or FUS mutations.
source: While removal of SARM1 does not alleviate motor neuron degeneration in a SOD1 model of ALS (Peters et al., 2018), this could be explained by the finding that TDP-43 aggregation is usually not seen in ALS linked to SOD1 or FUS mutations (Mackenzie et al., 2007; Maekawa et al., 2009; McAlary et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Of the 16 alleles encoding changes between amino acids 112 and 385 of the SARM1 ARM domain in Project MinE DF1, all are seen in patients.
source: Specifically, of the 16 alleles encoding changes between amino acids 112 and 385 of the SARM1 ARM domain, all are seen in patients, but only the two relatively more common alleles are also seen in controls, whereas the distribution of coding variation between patients and controls for the remainder of the gene is largely unremarkable, being much more proportional to the sizes of the patient and control groups.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: Only the two relatively more common ARM domain alleles are also seen in controls in Project MinE DF1.
source: Specifically, of the 16 alleles encoding changes between amino acids 112 and 385 of the SARM1 ARM domain, all are seen in patients, but only the two relatively more common alleles are also seen in controls, whereas the distribution of coding variation between patients and controls for the remainder of the gene is largely unremarkable, being much more proportional to the sizes of the patient and control groups.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: NAD+ levels are approximately halved in HEK 293T cells expressing exogenous WT SARM1.
source: Under these conditions, NAD+ levels are approximately halved in cells expressing exogenous WT SARM1 (due to overexpression of a low constitutive NADase activity) but we observed a substantially greater lowering of NAD+ for six of the ALS-specific variants - L223P, Δ229–235 (alternatively named Δ226–232 - see Table 1 legend), Δ249–252, V331E, E340K, and T385A SARM1 - suggestive of strong NADase GoF (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Six ALS-specific variants (L223P, Δ229–235, Δ249–252, V331E, E340K, and T385A SARM1) cause substantially greater lowering of NAD+ than WT SARM1 in HEK 293T cells.
source: Under these conditions, NAD+ levels are approximately halved in cells expressing exogenous WT SARM1 (due to overexpression of a low constitutive NADase activity) but we observed a substantially greater lowering of NAD+ for six of the ALS-specific variants - L223P, Δ229–235 (alternatively named Δ226–232 - see Table 1 legend), Δ249–252, V331E, E340K, and T385A SARM1 - suggestive of strong NADase GoF (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Three variants (V112I, A275V and A341V SARM1) showed smaller, but statistically-significant lowering of NAD+ compared to WT SARM1.
source: Smaller, but still statistically-significant lowering of NAD+ was also seen for a further three variants - V112I, A275V and A341V SARM1 - suggestive of more modest/moderate GoF.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The variants that had the strongest effect on NAD+ levels also caused greater depletion of NADP+ and ATP than WT SARM1.
source: The variants that had the strongest effect on NAD+ levels also caused greater depletion of NADP+ and ATP than WT SARM1 (Figure 2B,C), with NADP+ representing an alternative substrate of SARM1 glycohydrolase activity (Essuman et al., 2018; Horsefield et al., 2019; Wan et al., 2019) and ATP loss likely to be a lagging consequence of NAD+ loss.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: The variants that caused the greatest NAD+ depletion are barely detectable by immunoblotting.
source: Importantly, the lower level of NAD+ seen for some variants in these assays was not a result of greater variant overexpression. Instead, we found that the variants that caused the greatest NAD+ depletion are barely detectable by immunoblotting (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Enhanced NAD+ depletion is achieved by substantially lower levels of full-length versions of some of the variants.
source: This indicates that enhanced NAD+ depletion is achieved by substantially lower levels of full-length versions of some of the variants and suggests very strong GoF.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from the immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Five patient-specific variants (L223P, Δ229–235, Δ249–252, V331E and E340K) have constitutive NADase activity rates up to 20 times higher than WT SARM1.
source: Importantly, these assays confirmed the hypothesised NADase GoF for most of the variants that increased depletion of NAD+ in transfected HEK 293T cells, but in some cases, their constitutive activity was unexpectedly high: rates for five of the patient-specific variants - L223P, Δ229–235, Δ249–252, V331E and E340K - were found to be up to 20 times higher than WT SARM1 and a sixth - T385A - around 10 times higher (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by NADase activity assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: T385A SARM1 has constitutive NADase activity around 10 times higher than WT SARM1.
source: Importantly, these assays confirmed the hypothesised NADase GoF for most of the variants that increased depletion of NAD+ in transfected HEK 293T cells, but in some cases, their constitutive activity was unexpectedly high: rates for five of the patient-specific variants - L223P, Δ229–235, Δ249–252, V331E and E340K - were found to be up to 20 times higher than WT SARM1 and a sixth - T385A - around 10 times higher (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by NADase activity assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The very high per mol constitutive NADase activities of the six strong GoF variants are similar to that of SARM1 lacking the extreme N-terminus and auto-inhibitory ARM domain (SAM-TIR fragment).
source: In fact, these very high per mol constitutive NADase activities are similar to that of SARM1 lacking the extreme N-terminus and auto-inhibitory ARM domain (SAM-TIR fragment, amino acids 409–724) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by NADase activity assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: V112I SARM1 has a constitutive NADase activity rate a little more than twice as high as WT SARM1.
source: Of the three other variants that increased NAD+ depletion in transfected HEK 293T cells, V112I SARM1 has a rate a little more than twice as high as WT SARM1, whereas the activities of A275V and A341V SARM1 are not significantly raised (Figure 3A), although we cannot rule out subtle differences in the activities of the recombinant proteins compared to their activities in cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by NADase activity assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The constitutive NADase rates of P332Q and N337D SARM1 suggest partial loss-of-function.
source: Interestingly, the constitutive NADase rates calculated for P332Q and N337D, the variants present in both the patient and control groups, and R310H, a patient-specific variant, suggest partial LoF (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by NADase activity assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The NADase activity of WT SARM1 roughly tripled in the presence of 50 µM NMN.
source: Under these conditions, the NADase activity of WT SARM1 roughly tripled but there was no clear increase for the six variants with very high constitutive activity (L223P, Δ229–235, Δ249–252, V331E, E340K, and T385A SARM1) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by NADase activity assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was no clear increase in NADase activity for the six variants with very high constitutive activity (L223P, Δ229–235, Δ249–252, V331E, E340K, and T385A SARM1) in the presence of 50 µM NMN.
source: Under these conditions, the NADase activity of WT SARM1 roughly tripled but there was no clear increase for the six variants with very high constitutive activity (L223P, Δ229–235, Δ249–252, V331E, E340K, and T385A SARM1) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by NADase activity assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: V112I SARM1 showed no NMN-responsiveness.
source: On the other hand, V112I SARM1, which has moderately raised constitutive NADase activity, instead showed no NMN-responsiveness and its activity in the presence of 50 µM NMN is lower than the NMN-induced activity of WT SARM1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by NADase activity assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: R267W SARM1 is an additional strong gain-of-function variant identified in the Answer ALS database.
source: Using the same assays as for the original Project MinE variants, we identified patient-associated Answer ALS variant, R267W SARM1, as an additional strong GoF, with robust NAD+-consuming activity in transfected HEK 293T cells combined with low expression (Figure 4A and B) and a constitutively high, non-inducible NADase activity equivalent to that of the strongest Project MinE GoF variants (Figure 4C,E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figures 4A, 4B, 4C, and 4E.

claim: V88M SARM1 and A210V SARM1 reduced NAD+ levels more than WT SARM1 in transfected HEK 293T cells.
source: Interestingly, two of the control-associated variants, V88M SARM1 (Project MinE DF1) and A210V SARM1 (Answer ALS), also reduced NAD+ levels more than WT SARM1 in transfected HEK 293T cells (Figure 4A), but their constitutive activities in NADase assays were only modestly increased relative to WT SARM1 and far below the 10 times higher activity we define for strong GoF variants (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figures 4A and 4D.

claim: The constitutive activities of V88M SARM1 and A210V SARM1 in NADase assays were only modestly increased relative to WT SARM1.
source: Interestingly, two of the control-associated variants, V88M SARM1 (Project MinE DF1) and A210V SARM1 (Answer ALS), also reduced NAD+ levels more than WT SARM1 in transfected HEK 293T cells (Figure 4A), but their constitutive activities in NADase assays were only modestly increased relative to WT SARM1 and far below the 10 times higher activity we define for strong GoF variants (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: NAD+ depletion in HEK 293T cells co-transfected with equal amounts of WT and Δ229–235 SARM1 expression constructs was broadly similar to that in cells transfected with the Δ229–235 SARM1 construct alone.
source: We found that NAD+ depletion in HEK 293T cells co-transfected with equal amounts of WT and Δ229–235 SARM1 expression constructs was broadly similar to that in cells transfected with the Δ229–235 SARM1 construct alone (Figure 5A), although enzyme assays of the recombinant proteins are more effective at differentiating between moderate and high NADase GoF (see below).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Flag-tagged Δ229–235 SARM1 efficiently co-immunoprecipitates with HA-tagged WT SARM1 from co-expressing cells.
source: SARM1 readily homo-multimerises in solution to form an octameric ring structure (Gerdts et al., 2013; Horsefield et al., 2019; Sporny et al., 2019; Bratkowski et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2020; Sporny et al., 2020; Figley et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2021) and our finding that (Flag-tagged) Δ229–235 SARM1 efficiently co-immunoprecipitates with (HA-tagged) WT SARM1 from co-expressing cells is indicative that hetero-oligomers of WT and variant SARM1 are also readily formed (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The constitutive NADase activity of hetero-oligomers of WT and Δ229–235 SARM1 is intermediate between that of each protein alone.
source: Direct assaying of the NADase activity of hetero-oligomers revealed their constitutive NADase activity to be intermediate between that of each protein alone, but this still represents very strong GoF relative to WT SARM1 alone (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by NADase activity assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Substantially fewer DsRed labelled neurons were present 24 hr after injection with the Δ229–235 SARM1 construct compared to the WT SARM1 construct or empty vector.
source: A DsRed expression construct was co-injected to improve visualisation of the targeted neurons and their neurites (co-expression of ZsGreen from the SARM1 construct being insufficient under these conditions) and we consistently saw substantially fewer DsRed labelled neurons 24 hr after injection with the Δ229–235 SARM1 construct compared to the WT SARM1 construct or empty vector (Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: NR supplementation boosted DsRed expression and visualisation of the Δ229–235 SARM1 neurons.
source: We found that NR supplementation boosted DsRed expression and visualisation of the Δ229–235 SARM1 neurons (Figure 6A,B) suggesting that strong NADase GoF suppresses DsRed expression in neurons in the same way that it suppresses co-expression of ZsGreen in transfected HEK 293T cells (Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C), although a separate effect on neuronal viability also cannot be ruled out.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: The modest stresses associated with changes in culture conditions as a result of media change was sufficient to trigger a substantial loss of the Δ229–235 SARM1 neurons.
source: Intriguingly, we found that the modest stresses associated with changes in culture conditions as a result of media change, even to new NR-containing medium, was sufficient to trigger a substantial loss of the Δ229–235 SARM1 neurons (compared to not changing media), and further manipulations designed to reduce NAD+ biosynthesis – removal of NR, or a combination of NR removal and incubation with NAMPT inhibitor FK866 to block the rate-limiting step in the NAD+ salvage pathway – caused additional, incremental decreases in cell survival (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: Neurons injected with the WT SARM1 construct or empty vector were not substantially affected by manipulations designed to reduce NAD+ biosynthesis.
source: In contrast, neurons injected with the WT SARM1 construct or empty vector were not substantially affected by any of the manipulations (Figure 6C and D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: Double mutant Δ229–235/E642A SARM1 has little or no effect on NAD+ levels in transfected HEK 293T cells.
source: We found that double mutant Δ229–235/E642A SARM1, like single mutant E642A SARM1, has little or no effect on NAD+ levels in transfected HEK 293T cells (Figure 7A), consistent with a lack of NADase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: SCG neurons injected with a Δ229–235/E642A SARM1 construct were not sensitive to combined NR removal and incubation with NAMPT inhibitor FK866.
source: Crucially, in contrast to Δ229–235 SARM1, SCG neurons injected with a Δ229–235/E642A SARM1 construct were easily identified, even in the absence of NR supplementation, and were not sensitive to combined NR removal and incubation with NAMPT inhibitor FK866 (after being cultured in the presence of NR) (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: NADase activity is required for the pro-death effects of Δ229–235 SARM1.
source: Therefore, NADase activity is required for the pro-death effects of Δ229–235 SARM1 in this assay.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from the data showing that the NADase-dead Δ229–235/E642A SARM1 does not cause neuronal death.

claim: 13 of the 11,117 patients in the combined datasets are heterozygous for a strong GoF SARM1 allele.
source: Therefore, in total, 13 of the 11,117 patients in the combined datasets are heterozygous for a strong GoF SARM1 allele (13 out of 22,234 alleles), with no carriers among 10,402 controls (0 out of 20,804 alleles) (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: No carriers of strong GoF SARM1 alleles were found among 10,402 controls.
source: Therefore, in total, 13 of the 11,117 patients in the combined datasets are heterozygous for a strong GoF SARM1 allele (13 out of 22,234 alleles), with no carriers among 10,402 controls (0 out of 20,804 alleles) (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Burden testing of the group of seven strong GoF variant alleles together in the combined datasets revealed a highly significant association with disease (burden test and SKAT-O p = 0.00017).
source: Crucially, burden testing of the group of seven strong GoF variant alleles together in the combined datasets revealed a highly significant association with disease (burden test and SKAT-O p = 0.00017), whereas there was no clear association with disease when considering all the other alleles as a group (burden test p = 0.47, SKAT-O p = 0.61).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and represents statistical analysis of the aggregated data.

claim: There was no clear association with disease when considering all the other alleles as a group (burden test p = 0.47, SKAT-O p = 0.61).
source: Crucially, burden testing of the group of seven strong GoF variant alleles together in the combined datasets revealed a highly significant association with disease (burden test and SKAT-O p = 0.00017), whereas there was no clear association with disease when considering all the other alleles as a group (burden test p = 0.47, SKAT-O p = 0.61).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and represents statistical analysis of the aggregated data.

claim: There is a greater than four times enrichment of the strong GoF alleles among aggregated patient cohorts compared to European (non-Finnish) non-neuro samples from gnomAD v3.1.1 (MAF of 0.00058 vs 0.00014).
source: In addition, there is a greater than four times enrichment of the strong GoF alleles among our aggregated patient cohorts compared to European (non-Finnish) non-neuro samples from gnomAD v3.1.1 (Table 3 - MAF of 0.00058 vs 0.00014) and, despite the presence of a few carriers of strong GoF SARM1 alleles in this gnomAD cohort and the uncertainty regarding their health status (see Table 3 legend), their inclusion as additional controls in the statistical tests actually strengthens the association between the SARM1 strong GoF alleles and disease (burden test p = 0.000025, SKAT-O p = 0.000057).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Table 3.

claim: Two of the ALS cases are also heterozygous for I114T SOD1 and L17P FIG4 variant alleles that have previously been linked to ALS or recessive Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4 J (CMT4J).
source: In this respect it is notable that two of the ALS cases are also heterozygous for I114T (previously reported as I113T) SOD1 and L17P FIG4 variant alleles that have previously been linked to ALS or recessive Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4 J (CMT4J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by clinical information presented in Table 4.

claim: The I114T SOD1 allele shows incomplete penetrance.
source: Given that the I114T SOD1 allele shows incomplete penetrance (Lopate et al., 2010) and the L17P FIG4 allele has previously only been associated with CMT4J in combination with a null allele (Nicholson et al., 2011), it raises the possibility that an interaction with the SARM1 GoF alleles is critical for pathogenesis in these ALS cases.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The L17P FIG4 allele has previously only been associated with CMT4J in combination with a null allele.

evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Seven disease-associated SARM1 alleles encode missense or in-frame microdeletion variants with constitutive NADase activity as much as ten to twenty times higher than that of WT SARM1.
source: Here, we have identified seven disease-associated SARM1 alleles in patients with ALS or other motor nerve disorders that encode missense or in-frame microdeletion variants with constitutive NADase activity as much as ten to twenty times higher than that of WT SARM1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and summarizes the primary findings supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The level of constitutive NADase activity of the seven variants is comparable to that of SARM1 lacking any auto-inhibition.
source: This level of activity is comparable to that of SARM1 lacking any auto-inhibition and is substantially higher than the activity of WT SARM1 in the presence of NMN, a natural activator of SARM1 NADase during injury-induced and other related forms of axon degeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: The NADase activity of hetero-oligomers of WT and strong NADase GoF SARM1 will be around half that of homo-oligomers of strong GoF SARM1 alone.
source: Although co-expression experiments suggest that the NADase activity of hetero-oligomers of WT and strong NADase GoF SARM1 will be around half that of homo-oligomers of strong GoF SARM1 alone, this still represents a considerable increase in activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and inferred from the data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Acute expression of strong NADase GoF SARM1 alongside WT SARM1 in primary cultured neurons is sufficient to promote robust NADase-dependent cell death in response to otherwise non-harmful mild stress.
source: Consistent with this, acute expression of strong NADase GoF SARM1 alongside WT SARM1 in primary cultured neurons is sufficient to promote robust NADase-dependent cell death (and simultaneous or secondary axon degeneration) in response to otherwise non-harmful mild stress.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The seven strong GoF alleles are enriched in the motor nerve disorder cohorts studied compared to control groups or the wider population.
source: Crucially, these seven strong GoF alleles are enriched in the motor nerve disorder cohorts studied compared to control groups or the wider population implicating constitutively hyperactivated SARM1 as a risk factor for these diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data shown in Figure 8 and Table 3, and statistical analyses.

claim: The proportion of motor nerve disorder cases that are heterozygous for the strong GoF alleles identified is 0.12%.
source: Despite the robust association between SARM1 strong GoF variants and disease in these cohorts, the proportion of motor nerve disorder cases that are heterozygous for the strong GoF alleles identified here is only 0.12 %.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and calculated from the data presented in Figure 8.

claim: The lead SNP in an ALS GWAS study, rs35714695, is located only 8.3–11.4 kb from each of the strong GoF variants within the same ~200 kb linkage disequilibrium block.
source: While further replication in other cohorts is important, along with direct evidence that SARM1 activity is necessary for pathogenesis to firmly establish causation, the results presented here strongly implicate SARM1 as a risk factor in this group of diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to prior GWAS studies (Fogh et al., 2014; van Rheenen et al., 2016).
